title: The Flea and the Ox
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Flea once said to an Ox, "How comes it that a big strong fellow like you is content to serve mankind, and do all their hard work for them, while I, who am no bigger than you see, live on their bodies and drink my fill of their blood, and never do a stroke for it all?" To which the Ox replied, "Men are very kind to me, and so I am grateful to them: they feed and house me well, and every now and then they show their fondness for me by patting me on the head and neck." "They'd pat me, too," said the Flea, "if I let them: but I take good care they don't, or there would be nothing left of me."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Flea ask the Ox about?
options: Why the Ox never runs away from the farm
Why the Ox eats so much grass every day
Why the Ox is content to serve mankind and do their hard work
Why the Ox allows itself to be milked

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Flea say it does instead of working?
options: Lives on their bodies and drinks its fill of their blood
Hides quietly in the corners of their homes
Follows the Ox around all day watching it work
Steals scraps of food left on the table

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Ox say it is grateful to men?
options: Because they never ask him to work very hard
Because they let him roam freely without any fence
Because they protect him from other animals
Because they feed and house him well, and show fondness for him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do men show their fondness for the Ox?
options: By giving him a special name
By patting him on the head and neck
By decorating him with ribbons
By letting him lead the other animals

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Flea say men would do to it if it let them?
options: Feed it well, too
House it, too
Pat it, too
Protect it, too

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Flea take care that men don't touch it?
options: Because there would be nothing left of it
Because it dislikes being praised
Because it fears men will keep it as a pet
Because it wants to remain hidden from other fleas

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Flea's closing remark reveal a flaw in its own way of living?
options: It shows that the Flea secretly wants to be patted more than the Ox
It proves that men actually dislike the Flea more than the Ox
It suggests that the Flea plans to change its behavior soon
It admits that the same closeness to men that benefits the Ox would be fatal to it

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Ox's answer suggest about how it views its own hard work?
options: As an unfair burden it wishes it could escape
As a fair exchange for the care and affection it receives
As something forced upon it against its will
As a punishment for some past mistake

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Flea never does "a stroke" of work?
options: It works only a small amount
It works only at night
It does no work at all
It works only when forced to

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Closeness to those in power benefits the useful and endangers the merely parasitic
Fleas are always smarter than the animals they live on
Oxen should refuse to work no matter how well they are treated
Being small is always safer than being large

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Flea describe its own size compared to the Ox?
options: Almost as large as the Ox
Invisible to the naked eye
Larger than most other insects
No bigger than you see

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Ox say men do for it besides feeding it?
options: Groom its coat daily
House it well
Decorate its stall with flowers
Give it a special name

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Flea say would happen if it let men pat it?
options: It would become tame like the Ox
It would be given food in return
There would be nothing left of it
It would lose its ability to jump

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Ox's relationship with men be considered fundamentally different from the Flea's?
options: The Ox offers something valuable in return, while the Flea only takes without giving anything
The Ox is treated worse than the Flea despite working harder
The Flea provides more value to men than the Ox realizes
The Ox and the Flea are treated identically by men

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Flea seem to value most about its way of life?
options: Being praised and patted just like the Ox
Working hard to earn the trust of men
Living openly and honestly among men
Avoiding detection so it can continue taking without consequence

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "fondness" mean in "show their fondness for me"?
options: Anger or irritation
Affection or warm liking
Curiosity or interest
Fear or nervousness

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: An Ox convinces a Flea to start working for men as well
A Flea and an Ox agree that men treat them both unfairly
A Flea questions why an Ox works for men, and the Ox explains that its labor is repaid with kindness the Flea could never safely receive
An Ox complains to the Flea about being overworked
